recordings.text: I watched one piece settle where it touches several targets at once. A fork. Usually only one of them gets away.
I noticed a gap. One of their pieces can now reach several targets together, a fork waiting to happen.
In another move, one piece could have reached for several targets: a fork. It slipped by unplayed.
With its king standing behind it, that piece is held in place. Stepping off the line would open the king, so it stays very still.
Something tightens here. The other side can now pin a piece to its own king, and then it cannot step off that line.
Another move could have pinned one of theirs to its king, holding it on the line. Quietly, that pin went unused.
A skewer, neatly drawn. The front piece has to make way, and the piece it was hiding lies open.
Look down the line with me: the other side now holds a skewer, and once the front piece moves, the one behind it may be taken.
A skewer was sitting in a stronger move. Strike the front piece, and what hides behind it is uncovered. That chance drifted past.
Down goes the guard. Now look at the piece it was looking after; nothing watches it any more.
The other side can take a guard here. If it goes, the piece it was looking after stands uncovered.
A different move could have taken one of their guards, leaving its piece uncovered. That went by.
The king is fenced in by its own pieces along the back rank. The back-rank mate closes, softly.
The back rank needs a look. After this move, the other side has a way to mate there, with the king fenced in by its own pieces.
I saw mate on the back rank, with the enemy king fenced in by its own pieces. It went by, unplayed.
A pawn is on its way toward the last rank. Promotion is what it's walking toward.
One of their pawns has a road to the last rank now. I would keep my eyes on that one.
A stronger move would have started a pawn toward promotion. Here it stays at home, waiting.
One piece moves aside, and the piece behind it wakes and attacks. That's the discovered attack, working quietly.
Something is hidden behind one of their pieces. If it moves, the piece behind it attacks. That discovered attack now belongs to the other side.
A quiet discovered attack waited in another move: once the front piece moved, the one behind it would strike. It stayed hidden.
This one move carries two threats. A single answer rarely deals with them both.
Two threats can land together for the other side now, a double attack. Both have to be seen before a reply is chosen.
Two threats together were possible with a stronger move. Here the double attack waits unplayed.
The defender is coaxed off its post, and the thing it was guarding sits alone. A deflection, quietly done.
A defender can be coaxed away now. Watch what it guards; that is what would sit alone.
Another move could have coaxed a defender away from what it held. That deflection stayed in the drawer. See what the defender was minding.
Nothing was watching that piece, and now it's gone. The loose ones are always worth a first glance.
A piece with nothing watching it could have been taken with another move. This one leaves it on the board. A glance for loose pieces comes before anything else.
Nobody is watching one of the pieces now. The other side is free to pick it up.
I watched the defender walk away. It was the only real one, and what it guarded is open to capture now.
A threat came with their last move. I noticed it, though this move lets it be, and a piece is there to be captured.
On its own, the capture looks fine. Then comes the recapture, and it takes something of greater value. Count what comes back, not only what goes.
One of the minor pieces wakes and moves out. Small, but notice where it has settled.
Another move would have woken a minor piece and brought it off its home square.
The rook looks down an open file now, not one pawn of either color on it.
With another move, a rook would have had an open file, empty of pawns from end to end.
The rook's file has turned semi-open. Its own pawns are absent there; an enemy pawn or more still stands on it.
A different move would have handed a rook a semi-open file, empty of its own pawns, one of the enemy's still on it.
Passed, this pawn. Ahead of it, on its file and the two beside it, there is no enemy pawn at all.
With another move, a pawn would have been running free: no enemy pawn ahead of it on its file, nor on the files to either side.
On walks the passed pawn, a square nearer. I'd keep watching it.
With another move, the passed pawn could have stepped further along.
One pawn now stands isolated, no friend of its own color on either side. It stands by itself now.
With another move, a pawn would have stood isolated, no pawn of its color on the neighboring files.
That piece stood unwatched. Someone covers it now. Better.
With another move, an unwatched piece would have gained a guard of its own.
Nothing guards one of the pieces now. Worth noticing, though unguarded and lost are different things.
A different move would have left one piece unwatched, though that by itself would not hand it over.
The king has somewhere new to go, a legal square that was closed before. See what made room.
With another move, the king would have found a new legal square to step to. Look at what would have made space.
Castled: the king steps across, and the rook passes over to stand on the king's other side. A quiet pair of steps in a single move.
Castling was there instead: king and rook moving in a single turn.
One bishop goes, and the pair goes with it. That side can no longer watch both square colors with bishops.
With a different move, one of their two bishops would have been taken, and the pair would be gone.
One pawn now sits behind another of its own color on the same file: doubled. Notice how they stand.
Another move would have doubled a pair of pawns, one behind the other on one file.
Here is the turning point. From here, mate can be forced by the other side. Let's trace the attack back, slowly, to where the defense opened.
Mate was there, a forced one, and this move steps by it. The finish is worth going back to find.
Something is given away on purpose. Take it, and the idea still holds, in the line the engine checked. The offer stands.
Of all the moves examined, this was the only one that kept things playable; everything else went down. That was the narrow way, and this move took it.
The advantage lived through this move and no other; nothing else examined avoided a loss. A quiet, exact resource.
The reply comes quickly here. A capture is there for them straight away. Look there first.
Their strongest answer gives check. The king has to come first now.
The engine has its eye on a different move. Set it beside this one on the board and watch how the replies change.
The engine finds this weaker than its best move. Something slips away in the reply; look closely there.
Quietly strong. Of what the engine examined, this concedes very little.
Sound. The engine likes another a touch more, but most of the position's value is kept.
A recognized opening line, and this move has its place in it.
Here the game steps out of the opening book. From this move on, the position belongs to itself.
After the earlier setback, there's footing again: a playable position. Breathe; there's a way on.
After the earlier setback, things are playable once more, and the other side's errors helped open the way back.
Their last move left an opening, and you stepped into it. Nicely noticed.
An opening came with their last move, and this reply doesn't use it. One move back, there was something better waiting.
I've noticed this issue earlier in this game too. One warning sign, showing twice. Lay the moments next to each other.
Earlier a piece was left on its own; now someone is covering it again. Look at how its protection came back.
Little concessions keep gathering, and this is one more. Together they have worn the position thin.
The advantage stayed with that side, unbroken, until the recorded win. Walk back through that stretch; it was kept carefully.
I've seen this same issue in your other saved games. Look at them together.
Checkmate. There's no legal square left the king can reach. Finished, and cleanly.
Checkmate, and no legal move is left to the king. It's all right. Let's look back for the moment the defense could have held.
A draw. Nothing more to win or lose, though the moves along the way still have things to show.
Sit with the position a moment. Move when it comes clear.
Not quite. Look once more; it's still there to be found.
That attempt brought nothing back. Try the move again when you're ready.
There's a forced checkmate in the saved engine analysis, belonging to the side that made this move.
The saved engine analysis shows that, after this move, the other side can force checkmate.
Follow the saved line to its end, and the side that made this move finishes richer in material than it began.
Follow the saved line to its end, and the side that made this move finishes poorer in material than it began.
The exercise takes it. I can't see a clear tactical reason in the moves shown, and I won't invent one.
This one isn't accepted for the exercise, and the moves shown hold no clear tactical reason. Look again, slowly.
Yes, a saved answer, exactly. In this exercise, those answers are what count.
The saved answers for this exercise don't list that move. A legal move outside them isn't necessarily a poor one.
Let the move sit with you a moment before the next position.
Good. Hold on to why it works, not only to the move.
I've kept your practice. Nothing moves on the review schedule.
Solved. The relearning mark stays on it for now, and that's all right.
We begin here, in the position before any of these moves.
One more move. Notice what shifts.
Check. The king's trouble comes before every other thought.
And the king slips out of check.
The pawn reaches the far edge and turns into a new piece.
The pawn reaches the far edge and is promoted, and the new piece checks the king at once.
The pawn reaches the far edge and is promoted, and that is checkmate. No legal step is left to that king.
The pawn reaches the far edge and promotes, and its own king is out of check because of it.
A capture, and the board grows a little emptier.
A capture, and check with it.
A capture, and checkmate with it. Every square is closed to that king.
A capture, and the king is out of check with it.
The pawn takes a piece on its final step and promotes at the far edge.
Capturing as it goes, the pawn reaches the far edge, promotes, and gives check.
Capturing as it goes, the pawn reaches the far edge, promotes, and gives checkmate. Nowhere remains for that king.
Capturing as it goes, the pawn reaches the far edge and promotes, and its own king is freed from check.
The king castles, and with it comes check.
The king castles, and the game ends there in checkmate: the other king has nowhere it may go.
Watch one piece threaten several, then take one. In this example, the side with the fork ends ahead on material.
The marked capture isn't possible for that piece. Its king sits behind it on the line, and stepping off would leave the king exposed.
Pinned against its king, the attacked piece can't simply run. Wherever it goes, the king has to stay shielded.
With their own king behind them on the line, the defenders have to leave the capture alone. That's what makes it work, and the line shown wins material.
My eyes would stay on the pinned piece. It can't leave its line without baring its king, and before these moves finish, it's taken.
The front piece slides away. Behind it, along that same line, the next piece is captured.
The king has to answer the check by stepping aside, and the piece it was screening is taken by the same attacker.
First the one defender is captured, and then its piece. Notice how the first capture opens the way for the second.
The defender is coaxed off its post, and the piece it protected is captured.
The blocker moves, a line opens, and the piece behind it captures along that line.
A piece slips out of the way, and from behind it comes check.
Double check. With two pieces checking together, only a king move can answer.
One attack from the piece that moves, and a second from the line it opens. Here, it's that second attack that wins its target.
Watch the pawn reach promotion. In this example that side ends with more material, too.
Nothing guarded that piece, so it's taken. In this example the capturing side ends ahead on material.
The opponent's last move let a relative pin go, and the attacking piece was free. Its target never moved away, and the line shown ends with that target captured.
That marked reply is open to the other side. Set it on the board, and the next position will tell you more.
Before you move, glance over your own pieces for anything that could be taken for free.
Before a quiet move, let your eyes sweep the board for loose enemy pieces.
Among the forcing moves, notice any single piece that could reach two valuable targets.
Every pin hides something behind the pinned piece. Before it moves, find out whether that's your king or a piece worth more.
Let your eye travel past the first target. Something valuable may wait behind it on the line.
Before a defender is traded off, notice what it's quietly protecting.
When a piece is blocking a line, notice what that line would reach if it moved.
Watch for a single move with two threats in it, counting checks and lines that open.
Before a back-rank defender moves, make sure your king can still breathe.
Measure how far a pawn has left to promotion, and notice which pawn moves force an answer.
Before a defender moves, notice which pieces it was quietly covering.
Before capturing, set what you win beside what the recapture would win back.
Notice when a forcing exchange might coax a defender off a second job.
What this exercise accepts is set by its saved answers. Other legal moves aren't wrong chess just for being left out.
What you see here is play against strong replies. Strong isn't the same as forced.
Material changes here count only within the line shown, from where it began. You'll find the piece values in the written explanation.
I find no simple tactical reason in the saved line, and I haven't guessed at a positional one. Walk through it yourself and set the replies side by side.

The whole solution, and not one wrong move. Lovely.

Known, again.
Known once more. Being in the book tells us where we stand; the move's quality is another question.

I'm Juniper. I look for what a move leaves unguarded, and when I see it, I'll tell you, gently.
So still, before anything moves. I like a board this calm, even knowing it won't last.
Not quite what this chapter is asking for, I'm afraid. Look again, softly; it's still waiting for you.
